name: don-johnson
style: American male documentary narrator telling a true story to a friend. Calm, confident, a little amused, brisk pace around 200 words per minute, clear on every word. Numbers are crisp and land. "No." is one flat word after a beat. The last line is a quiet, dry question. No hype, no shouting.

lines.text: You run a casino, and your biggest customer wants a discount on every dollar he loses.
It's late twenty ten in Atlantic City.
The recession has thinned out the high rollers.
One whale's night can decide whether a casino's month ends in the red.
So the casinos start fighting for whales with discounts.
Don Johnson used to run a racetrack.
He started at twenty-five dollar tables.
Now he bets a hundred thousand a hand.
And he won't play until the casino agrees to his terms.
Six decks.
The dealer stands on soft seventeen.
He can split aces again.
Rule by rule, the house edge shrinks to about a quarter of one percent.
Then the big one.
Lose more than half a million, and the casino hands back twenty percent.
Lose a million, and two hundred thousand comes back.
His losing nights now cost less.
His winning nights still pay in full.
December, Caesars: about four point two million dollars.
Then the Borgata: about five million.
April, the Tropicana: five point eight million in twelve hours.
One hand alone paid eight hundred thousand.
It's the worst loss in the Tropicana's history.
That's about fifteen million in six months.
Caesars bans him.
Other casinos turn him away.
So he must count cards, right?
No.
He plays by the book, and luck still matters.
But the edge was never in his head.
The casinos wrote it into the deal themselves.
The Tropicana and the Borgata stopped offering him those terms.
So when a casino offers you a deal, who do you think did the math first?
